#2092. Three Defeats And Gone: What Křetínský’s History Means For Nuno

West Ham supporters wondering how long Daniel Křetínský will continue backing Nuno Espírito Santo might find some surprising answers in the Czech billionaire’s history at Sparta Prague. Because while the Hammers manager currently appears secure in his position, Křetínský has previously been involved in managerial decisions that make Nuno’s recent difficulties look relatively modest.

In one particularly extraordinary example, Sparta dismissed a manager despite being nine points clear at the top of the league. Another departed following three damaging defeats in quick succession.

And having looked into Křetínský’s history, I’m beginning to wonder whether Nuno’s position at West Ham is quite as secure as many of us have assumed.

Kretinsky has a history of being ruthless with underperforming coaches

Křetínský became involved in Sparta Prague’s ownership and management in 2004, when investment group J&T acquired the club. He subsequently became chairman and has overseen an extraordinary number of managerial changes.

Perhaps the most remarkable came in December 2004, when František Straka was dismissed despite Sparta being nine points clear at the top of the Czech league.

Yes, you read that correctly. Nine points clear.

Even more interestingly, Křetínský explained the decision himself in an October 2008 interview with Czech newspaper iDNES.

The club’s sporting leadership had lost confidence in Straka’s footballing system. With Champions League qualification looking secure, Křetínský decided to make the change early to give a replacement time to prepare.

He subsequently admitted the decision was a mistake.

Nevertheless, it provides an extraordinary insight into his thinking. League position alone was not enough to protect a manager if Křetínský lacked confidence in his methods.

The example I found particularly interesting was Vítězslav Lavička, whose first spell as Sparta manager lasted just 123 days in 2008.

Lavička had started reasonably well, but three damaging defeats in quick succession changed everything.

Sparta lost 3-0 against Slovan Liberec, suffered European elimination against Dinamo Zagreb and were then thrashed 4-1 by Slavia Prague.

Lavička subsequently left the club, with the departing coach explaining that he had rejected conditions attached to his continued employment.

So this wasn’t quite a straightforward dismissal. Nevertheless, three damaging results had helped bring a very short managerial reign to an abrupt end.

Considering West Ham have just suffered consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, I find that particularly interesting.

In February 2021, Sparta dismissed Václav Kotal despite the club sitting second in the Czech league.

In Sparta’s official announcement, sporting director Tomáš Rosický explained that management believed the team’s objectives were under threat and performances were deteriorating.

In other words, second place wasn’t considered sufficient protection when the club believed things were heading in the wrong direction.

Similarly, when Lavička returned for a second spell, he was dismissed in April 2015 with Sparta five points behind the league leaders and several seasonal objectives already missed.

These later decisions were made within Sparta’s wider management structure, so it would be wrong to suggest Křetínský personally ordered every dismissal.

A loss against Cardiff could spell danger for Nuno

Until now, I’ve been fairly convinced that Nuno is extremely secure in his job.

After all, it was Křetínský who backed the manager during the summer despite David Sullivan apparently wanting a change.

My assumption was that having made such a significant decision, the Czech billionaire would be reluctant to admit he had backed the wrong man.

Having researched his Sparta Prague history, I’m no longer so sure.

There is nothing in that record to suggest Křetínský will necessarily stick with a manager simply because he appointed or supported him.

If anything, what he has consistently demonstrated is a willingness to sanction managerial change when his club’s principal objectives appear to be slipping away.

At Sparta, that generally meant winning titles or securing European qualification.

At West Ham, the equivalent objective is automatic promotion back to the Premier League.

And having dropped to eighth in the Championship, following another dreadful home defeat, Nuno certainly isn’t making that task look particularly straightforward.

Of course, Sparta Prague and West Ham have different ownership structures, and none of this proves Křetínský is currently considering dismissing Espírito Santo.

But it has changed my assessment of the situation.

I no longer believe Nuno can necessarily survive a sustained period outside the automatic promotion places.

And if Křetínský’s history tells us anything, it’s that backing a manager today offers no guarantee he’ll still be backing him tomorrow.

#2091. ‘Not ready’ – Liverpool told to forget about partaking in title race after Arsenal reality check

Liverpool aren’t yet ready to mount a serious Premier League title challenge this season, despite signs of ‘progress’ under Andoni Iraola.

That’s according to Ian Ladyman in his column for the Daily Mail after the Reds lost 1-0 at home to Arsenal on Sunday, a result which leaves the Merseysiders nine points behind the reigning champions with just under a quarter of the campaign having been played.

It was a second defeat at Anfield in the last month for LFC, who were also beaten by second-placed Manchester City in a game which swung on the incredibly harsh dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch.

In taking stock of viable Premier League title contenders, Ladyman wrote in his Monday column: ‘As for Liverpool, they are simply not ready. Not yet.

‘That was apparent before yesterday’s home defeat to Arsenal, in which they played well. Andoni Iraola’s team also played nicely at home to City last month but lost that one too.’

The journalist added that ‘there has been progress’ under the Basque, particuarly in terms of their defence, but he feels that the Reds ‘remain a puzzle in the final third’ and lack a ‘calm intelligence and threat just when it really matters’.

In terms of realistic aspirations for Liverpool this season, Ladyman outlined: ‘A third-placed finish, a journey to the last eight of the Champions League and a tilt at a domestic cup would represent progress for Liverpool.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

A win for the Reds would’ve put them within three points of the summit and fuelled talk of potential title race involvement, especially as beating Arsenal would’ve represented a significant statement.

Instead, a gap of nine points this early in the season indicates that Liverpool are unlikely to be contending for the Premier League trophy after Easter. A return of just one home win out of five in the top flight also shows how short we are compared to the Gunners and Man City.

On the whole, Iraola’s side have shown discernible improvement since the extended international break earlier in the autumn compared to how they played prior to that three-week hiatus, with signs that the head coach’s tactical ideas are starting to click with the squad.

The performances against Arsenal and Man City were creditable, and in both games we were wronged by scandalous refereeing decisions, but the results show that there’s still a gap to be bridged to the top two.

If Liverpool end the season comfortably in third place, go deep in the Champions League and hopefully lift a domestic cup, that’d represent a successful first campaign for Iraola at Anfield.

Nobody had us in the title equation back in August, and that remains the case now, but at least the way the Reds are playing would suggest that they’re gradually heading in the right direction under the current head coach.

#2090. West Ham Sack Nuno As Křetínský Loses Patience

West Ham United have confirmed that Nuno Espírito Santo has been sacked with immediate effect following mounting pressure on the Hammers head coach over the past few days.

The Portuguese manager’s position had become increasingly precarious following consecutive defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, with concerns growing behind the scenes that the club’s automatic promotion ambitions were slipping away.

As Claret & Hugh reported earlier, there had been growing indications from within the club that Nuno was no longer safe in his position. Daniel Křetínský was understood to be increasingly unimpressed with performances, and the decision to act suggests the West Ham hierarchy were no longer prepared to allow the situation to continue.

Rumours had also emerged yesterday that discussions were already taking place over the identity of West Ham’s next head coach, suggesting that preparations for a possible managerial change were underway.

The decision is particularly significant given Křetínský’s previous backing of Nuno. However, as our earlier research into his managerial decisions at Sparta Prague demonstrated, the Czech billionaire has a history of making changes when he believes a club’s objectives are under threat.

West Ham have now confirmed that the change has been made following a review of the Championship campaign.

In an official statement, the club announced:

West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team Head Coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect.

Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the Board of Directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the Club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.

Assistant Head Coach Rui Pedro Silva and Goalkeeper Coach Rui Barbosa have also departed.

West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the Club, and wish them all the very best for the future.

The process of recruiting a new Head Coach is already underway.

Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of squad preparations ahead of tomorrow evening’s EFL Championship fixture at Cardiff City, and the Club will make no further comment until the appointment of the new Head Coach is confirmed.

West Ham must now move quickly to appoint a replacement, with the Championship promotion race continuing and tomorrow night’s trip to Cardiff City fast approaching.

#2088. West Ham Insider Reveals Nuno’s Striker Gamble Before Sacking

Following the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo, questions are inevitably being asked about what went wrong during his time at West Ham United. And while there are plenty of areas worth examining, one of the most revealing concerns the Hammers’ striking department.

As Claret & Hugh learned from a West Ham insider before Nuno’s departure, the club’s three recognised centre-forwards were all specifically wanted by the Portuguese coach. That information is particularly significant given the team’s struggles in front of goal and the manager’s apparent reluctance to use some of the players he recruited.

The source’s assessment was straightforward: “They were all Nuno’s picks.”

It is a revelation that makes some of the decisions taken during the Championship campaign even harder to understand, particularly now that the manager has paid the price for West Ham’s disappointing performances.

The transfers attributed to recruitment director Nils Koppen have enjoyed varying degrees of success, and I still believe the jury is out on whether West Ham overpaid for Arne Engels.

But as Koppen himself explained, he had a very short period of time at the London Stadium before the summer transfer window closed.

What is not in doubt, according to our source, is that Nuno wanted Taty Castellanos, Pablo and Joël Piroe.

And it is the situation surrounding Piroe that I find particularly interesting.

“Nuno pushed really hard for Piroe because of his Championship goalscoring record. I’m surprised he hasn’t played more.”

Nuno pushed hard for Piroe but didn’t play him

Piroe arrived with a proven record of scoring goals in the Championship, something West Ham desperately needed following relegation.

Yet despite the Hammers’ continuing struggles in front of goal, he was given relatively limited opportunities to establish himself.

If Nuno was so determined to sign him, why was he so reluctant to play him?

It’s a perfectly reasonable question, particularly when neither Castellanos nor Pablo has done enough to make himself indispensable.

As we have already highlighted, the constant chopping and changing in attack did little to help any of West Ham’s forwards find form.

And if all three were Nuno’s preferred signings, it becomes considerably harder to blame the recruitment department for the lack of goals.

There had also been growing concern behind the scenes at the London Stadium that Espírito Santo did not know his best team.

It was a criticism supporters had been making for some time, and one that became increasingly difficult to dismiss as the manager continued changing personnel and formations.

The defeat against West Bromwich Albion provided another example of a team struggling for cohesion, creativity and confidence.

Ordinarily, in times gone by at West Ham, a certain amount of player frustration would eventually find its way back to David Sullivan.

Whether that happened in this instance remains unclear, particularly given the uncertainty surrounding the club’s ownership and decision-making structure.

But irrespective of any input from players, it had become increasingly evident that concerns were growing within the Hammers hierarchy.

The subsequent decision to dismiss Nuno confirms that the board believed a change was necessary, although it does not establish which individual concerns proved decisive.

Of course, Nuno’s departure doesn’t magically solve West Ham’s goalscoring problems.

Castellanos, Pablo and Piroe remain at the club, and whoever takes over will have to find a way of getting considerably more from them.

But that is also what makes the appointment of a new manager so interesting.

We have spent months wondering whether the problem was the players themselves or the way they were being used.

Now somebody else will have an opportunity to find out.

And perhaps the most revealing test will be what happens to Piroe, the proven Championship goalscorer whom Nuno apparently wanted so badly but seemed so reluctant to select.

#2087. No case for defence if Neil McCann can't turn around kamikaze Kilmarnock quickly

When Gary Neville’s Valencia side conceded a seventh goal to Barcelona, the camera cut to the Manchester United legend standing in his technical area looking ashen faced, utterly bereft.

As you took in his befuddled expression, helpless to prevent the car crash unfolding before him, you couldn’t help but wonder if he would have the gall to soon be back on the Sky Sports couch, telling others how to do the job he had just so miserably failed in.

Of course he did. And that spell in charge of what, admittedly, at the time, was an absolute basket case of a club, has been used as a stick with which to beat him ever since.

If things ultimately don’t work out for Neil McCann at Rugby Park – and it is starting to look as though that may be the case – I am sure he too will be back in the BBC Sportsound studio before you know it. And rightly so. McCann is an engaging and insightful pundit. The qualities that make a good, entertaining football analyst don’t necessarily make a top-class manager, though.

But then, I would say that. I too am paid to give my opinions on the beautiful game, and the highlight of my own managerial career – about half a season as player/manager of Motherwell Phoenix in the Carluke & District Sunday league – was a solitary 3-2 win amid a barrage of hungover batterings. Take that, Lanark Youth.

It would be massively unfair too and disrespectful in fact to dismiss McCann as a pundit turned manager, given his vast experience in the game as a hugely talented player and his previous managerial stints at Dundee, Inverness on an interim basis, as well as his time at Rangers as part of Barry Ferguson’s backroom team.

However, as McCann himself will know having been part of the Scottish football media set, his performance as manager of Kilmarnock will justifiably be subject to the same sort of scrutiny he used to apply to others, and at the risk of drawing a similarly icy stare to the one he fixed on former BBC colleague Chick Young at the weekend when he asked if McCann was feeling the pressure, any objective analysis would have to conclude that things are not going so peachily at present.

Killie currently sit in 11th place in the table, a point ahead of Hibs, who have a game in hand. Most concerningly, they are shipping goals for fun, conceding 2.3 per game so far this term, comfortably the worst record in the division. They have lost eight goals more than anyone else, letting in 28 across their 12 games to Motherwell and St Mirren’s 20. Their goal difference of -15 puts them seven worse off than the closest side, the Saints again, in that column.

McCann has been round the block often enough to know that the team who ships the most goals over the course of a campaign usually goes down. On only four occasions in the Premiership era have the side who conceded the most goals survived, with two of those doing so via the playoffs after finishing 11th. Never has the team with the worst defence in the league finished higher than 10th, which has also happened just twice.

Surely, stumbling to safety, whether that be through the playoffs or by scraping into tenth place, isn’t the limit of Kilmarnock’s ambitions this term? If they continue on their current trajectory, though, and carry on defending so poorly, then not only will that be their ceiling, it also seems a bit of a reach. Across McCann’s time at the club, in fact, Killie have conceded 53 goals in 22 league games, a record that is surely unsustainable.

It would be remiss not to mention though that many of those games came after he walked into an absolutely dire predicament in January following a run of 10 games without a victory under predecessor Stuart Kettlewell. That extended to 14 games under interim boss Kris Doolan before club owner Billy Bowie sent out the SOS to McCann and assistant Billy Dodds in early January.

Kilmarnock were also 11th at that time, just three points ahead of bottom side Livingston, who had a game in hand. Had you offered any Killie fan the playoff spot at that stage, they might have bitten your hand off like a, well, hungry squirrel, but McCann managed to turn things around despite the make-up of the squad not being suited to his preferred 4-2-3-1 formation, and he secured the Rugby Park side’s safety with a game to spare.

It is fair to say then that the many sceptics who gave his appointment in the winter window a frosty reception were mainly won over by the fine job he did in the remainder of the campaign.

There was a great deal of optimism around in the summer, in fact, that having had the opportunity to build a squad in his image, that the issues such as the leaky defence that had plagued Killie would be ironed out, and all the while, he would retain the front-footed approach that had been so refreshing during his first months in charge.

The balance, though, is still way off kilter. While Killie still look decent going forward at times and play some nice stuff, there is no way of dressing up their persistent issues at the back. Their defending at times is absolutely criminal, and you can't be in a position where you need to score three times in a game just to have a chance of winning.

McCann held his hands up to a naïve approach when Celtic came and plundered four first half goals in an eventual 5-1 win at Rugby Park back in August, but naïve barely covers the way that his team twice gave up a lead against 10-man St Johnstone on Saturday.

The second goal in particular had to be seen to be believed. A Killie corner somehow led, within seconds, to an opposition player running through on goal, with the set-up behind the ball leaving the hosts wide open. Even then, in fairness to the Killie manager, his defenders should have done much better when they got back at Joel Cotterill, but three retreating Killie men allowed him to waltz through on Nico Mantl unhindered before finding the net to howls of derision from the home stands.

And therein lies the growing issue for McCann. The boos are getting louder week upon week. While it could be argued that he deserves a bit of time to correct the defensive issues his team are facing after the escape act he pulled off last season, the more that his side display the same consistent weaknesses, the less faith there is from the Killie support that he can pull their team out of another mess. This time, one of his own making.

In the end, it won’t be his erstwhile colleagues in the media that seal his fate, but those paying – and increasingly, braying – punters. If he doesn’t want to be back at Pacific Quay any time soon, he has to find a way to bolt the back door.

There are no guarantees of course that changing manager mid-season would help pull Kilmarnock out of this death spiral they are currently in. Though, admittedly, it did work for them the last time they tried it.

Time is surely running out for McCann to avoid being on the other side of that scenario.

#2085. ‘Really poor’ – Steven Gerrard left raging over ‘absolute embarrassment’ at Anfield on Sunday

Steven Gerrard described the failure of Stuart Attwell on VAR to intervene over a crucial decision at Anfield on Sunday as ‘an absolute embarrassment’.

There was controversy in the 21st minute of Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal when Jurrien Timber pulled Alexander Isak’s shirt inside the penalty area, a clear foul which somehow went unpunished just five minutes after Kai Havertz’s winning goal.

Reds boss Andoni Iraola went as far as to suggest that he’d encourage his players to go to ground in such situations, with the Swedish striker staying on his feet and not protesting to the referee despite the obvious offence on him.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily, Gerrard was aghast at how Attwell on VAR failed to intervene over the incident involving Timber and Isak.

The ex-Liverpool captain said: “The speed of the cross and how it happened and the reaction, you can understand how a referee could possibly miss that or think there’s not much in that, but for someone to sit in [the VAR room] with all these screens around – how you miss that in the VAR seat is an absolute embarrassment.”

He added: “To hold someone’s shirt for that long and have three or four opportunities to see that and slow it down, and the amount of cameras that are in stadia at the moment, it’s really poor from Stuart Attwell.”

It will coast West Ham just under £3m to sack Rui Pedro Silva & Nuno Espirito Santo

In effect, Parker’s longer-term future at West Ham will depend upon achieving promotion this season.

#2083. Ruthless Křetínský Refuses To Gamble His West Ham Reputation On Nuno Any Longer

Daniel Křetínský has demonstrated that there is a limit to how far he is prepared to gamble his reputation at West Ham United on Nuno Espírito Santo. Having backed the Portuguese coach during the summer, the Czech billionaire has now seen the club abandon that decision following a disappointing start to the Championship campaign.

It represents a significant change of direction for West Ham, particularly given the circumstances surrounding Nuno’s retention after relegation. David Sullivan had reportedly favoured a managerial change, but Křetínský supported the idea of continuity and giving the existing head coach an opportunity to lead the promotion campaign.

At the time, I could understand the argument, even if I wasn’t convinced by it. But following consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, West Ham’s board has now decided that the situation cannot continue.

There was always an element of risk attached to retaining Nuno following relegation.

He had failed to keep West Ham in the Premier League, but the argument for keeping him was that he knew the squad, understood the club and could provide the stability needed for an immediate return.

Unfortunately, that stability never really materialised.

West Ham have spent much of the Championship campaign struggling to establish a recognisable playing style, with the manager regularly changing formations and personnel.

And despite the considerable talent available to him, Nuno appeared increasingly unable to get the best out of his players.

The 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion was particularly damaging because it exposed so many of the problems supporters had been highlighting for months.

The team looked disorganised, short of confidence and heavily reliant on Jarrod Bowen to produce something out of nothing.

It was hardly the performance of a side looking capable of securing automatic promotion.

Kretinsky was not prepared to back Espirito Santo any longer

The decision to retain Nuno was never simply about the manager.

West Ham had already committed themselves to a huge financial gamble following relegation, selling a substantial amount of their most valuable talent while attempting to rebuild a squad capable of returning to the Premier League.

There was an understandable desire to reduce costs, but also an expectation that the club would use its remaining resources wisely.

And that is where Nuno’s continued struggles became particularly worrying.

Having sold so much of the family silver during the summer, West Ham cannot simply assume they will get another opportunity to flex their financial muscle in the Championship.

A second season outside the Premier League could present an entirely different challenge.

The club needs good coaching, sensible recruitment and a clear tactical identity.

As Nils Koppen’s plans for a recognisable West Ham footballing identity demonstrated, there is already an ambition to establish something more sustainable.

But that was becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the football being produced under Nuno.

What I found particularly interesting when researching Křetínský’s history at Sparta Prague was his willingness to change managers when a club’s objectives appeared to be under threat.

At Sparta, those objectives generally involved winning titles or securing Champions League football.

At West Ham, the immediate equivalent is automatic promotion.

I had previously assumed that because Křetínský backed Nuno during the summer, he would be reluctant to abandon that decision.

His Sparta record made me reconsider that assumption.

Of course, we should distinguish the board’s collective decision from any suggestion that Křetínský personally ordered Nuno’s dismissal. The club has not publicly established who drove the final decision.

Nevertheless, the outcome is clear. The manager Křetínský reportedly wanted to retain is no longer in charge.

Křetínský’s reputation will not ultimately be judged on whether he supported Nuno for a few months too long.

It will be judged on whether West Ham can get back into the Premier League.

And having taken the decision to change managers, the board now has to ensure the next appointment gives the club the best possible opportunity to achieve that objective.

There is still plenty of talent in this squad, and I remain convinced a better-organised team could produce considerably more convincing performances.

West Ham have made their decision. Now they need to make sure it was worth making.

#2082. (Video) Half-time tunnel footage from Anfield on Sunday will only add to Liverpool fans’ fury

Liverpool fans’ sense of injustice over their defeat at Anfield on Sunday will be compounded by footage from the tunnel during half-time.

Arsenal triumphed 1-0 courtesy of a 16th-minute Kai Havertz goal, but the main talking point came five minutes later when Jurrien Timber pulled Alexander Isak’s shirt inside the penalty area and somehow avoided any sanction.

The failure of referee Andy Madley and VAR Stuart Attwell to award a spot kick caused widespread fury, with Jamie Carragher screaming at the officials to ‘do your job‘ and Steven Gerrard describing the situation as ‘an absolute embarrassment‘.

As if that inexplicable oversight wasn’t galling enough for Liverpool fans, there has now been footage shared of an exchange between Madley and Arsenal defender Gabriel in the Anfield tunnel at half-time.

In a clip posted by @LFC_Oman on X (via the Daily Briefing), the referee appears to tell the Brazil international: “Gabriel, be careful, yeah? You have already got two fouls.”

The whistler is then seen smiling and laughing after that quick word to the 28-year-old, followed by the two men sharing a momentary fist bump as the players ran out onto the pitch.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Maybe it was nothing more than a harmless exchange between Madley and Gabriel, but in the context of how the match went on Sunday, this clip will only add fuel to the fire from a Liverpool perspective.

If indeed the referee dished out a brief heads-up to the Arsenal defender, it could be perceived as him deviating from the neutrality he’s supposed to maintain, and the manner in which those involved were smiling after his words makes it seem like they were being too friendly with each other.

Also, that it was swiftly followed by a fist bump makes it seem even less professional from the official in particular, and he should’ve exercised more awareness in recognising that there were 60,000 or so home fans at Anfield already on his case over the failure to award a penalty for Timber’s blatant foul on Isak.

Madley should be less interested in sharing friendly chats with one team’s players inside the tunnel at half-time and more focused on his own performance and what he could’ve done better on the day.

This footage will only add to the prevailing sentiment among football fans in this country that refereeing standards at Premier League level leave an awful lot to be desired, especially for a division which is often proclaimed with chest-out bravado as the best domestic league in the world.

#2081. West Ham Have Hired A Championship Specialist – And I’m Delighted

A lot has already been written about incoming West Ham manager Scott Parker, and I make absolutely no apologies for being excited about his appointment.

To be crystal clear, Parker probably wouldn’t have been my first choice. But I’d reached the conclusion that Nuno Espírito Santo was incapable of taking West Ham forward, and with the club desperately needing to revive its Championship promotion campaign, a change was essential.

Is Scott Parker capable of doing that? Absolutely. As Claret & Hugh has confirmed through its own sources at West Ham, Parker is set to become the Hammers’ new head coach. And I believe there are two particular qualities that could make him exactly what this team needs.

I understand there are reservations about Parker’s record in the Premier League, and perhaps even the football his Burnley team played during their most recent promotion campaign.

After all, Burnley had the meanest defence in the Championship, and some supporters are understandably concerned that West Ham might be replacing one cautious manager with another.

But far from viewing that defensive record as a negative, I’d suggest West Ham desperately need somebody capable of improving our back line.

We’ve looked disorganised defensively for far too long, and a manager who can actually get players defending properly would be a welcome change.

Espirito Santo could not fix West Ham’s defence

Not that I want us to be boring, of course.

I also believe Parker is capable of getting more out of the players in attack, particularly the likes of Jarrod Bowen, Divine Mukasa and Lewis Orford.

And there’s something else worth remembering.

Parker has achieved promotion from the Championship with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley. Three promotions with three different clubs.

That’s not a bad record for somebody being brought in to do precisely the same job at West Ham.

I’m often reminded of something former Blackburn Rovers manager Mark Hughes said about signing striker Roque Santa Cruz.

Hughes explained that he’d watched the player countless times but decided to concentrate on what he could do rather than obsessing over his flaws.

It’s something that has always stuck in my mind.

And I think it’s particularly relevant when assessing Parker.

Rather than concentrating exclusively on his shortcomings, I’d prefer to focus on two qualities that I believe could make an enormous difference at West Ham.

Parker is an infectious character and a motivational speaker. He’s somebody who communicates with passion and conviction, and I believe that alone could make a considerable difference to this squad.

In short, I think he’s a far better communicator than Nuno Espírito Santo.

That might sound like a relatively small thing, but I don’t believe it is.

West Ham have looked like a team lacking confidence, direction and motivation for much of this season.

A manager who can get his message across clearly and make players believe in what they’re doing could transform performances without changing a single member of the squad.

One of my biggest frustrations with Espírito Santo was his apparent inability to address West Ham’s dreadful starts to football matches.

Time and again, we’d begin games slowly, allow opponents to take control and then spend the rest of the afternoon trying to recover.

It was a problem Nuno repeatedly acknowledged but never seemed capable of fixing.

And I suspect motivation played a significant part in that.

Whatever else people might say about Parker, I find it difficult to imagine his players routinely wandering onto the pitch looking half asleep. He’ll have them fired up, motivated and ready to compete from the opening whistle.

Of course, enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to win football matches.

But Parker also has the tactical experience to back it up.

He’s demonstrated that he understands the Championship, knows how to organise a team and can put together a successful promotion campaign.

I certainly don’t expect him to be out-thought tactically by virtually every opposition manager, which increasingly appeared to be the case under Nuno.

And while there will undoubtedly be questions about how Parker’s methods translate to the Premier League, that’s a discussion for another day.

We’re in the Championship, and our immediate priority is getting out of it.

Scott Parker has already demonstrated on three separate occasions that he knows exactly how to do that.

In short, Scotty P understands this Championship stuff considerably better than Nuno ever appeared to.

And I don’t see too much wrong with appointing a specialist for the job.

#2079. Andoni Iraola: Liverpool cannot ‘sustain the level’ I want

Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

“We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

“We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Alisson, Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo all made their first appearances and contributed to a lively first-half in which Iraola’s commitment to man-to-man marking and an intensive pressing structure were evident out of possession. With the ball in the first half they demonstrated the kind of slick passing that Bournemouth employed to carve opponents open on the counter-attack.

A nimble one-two between Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai allowed the Dutch midfielder to set up Alexander Isak to score with a shot from 16 yards and the most expensive player in English football history laid claim to the second, too, when he seemed to hook in a rebound from Lukas Hradecky’s save while lying in the six-yard box.

Later he would graciously acknowledge that he and Florian Wirtz had connected with the ball simultaneously and he was happy to yield the credit to his team-mate.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

At that point it seemed that victory would be a cakewalk but just before half-time Aleksandr Golovin caught Van Dijk out with a feint and late swerve to the right, tripping over the Liverpool captain’s clumsy hack. Despite a heavy limp, Golovin hammered the penalty past Alisson’s dive to make it 2-1 at the break.

Iraola rationed his early changes at the start of the second half to two but Liverpool could not regain their rhythm and Mika Biereth capitalised on a Gravenberch error to score the equaliser after battling to be first to the rebound when Giorgi Mamardashvili saved his first effort, stroking his effort through Wataru Endo’s legs.

Cue five substitutions as soon as that goal had gone in and a raft more followed, killing the remaining half-hour of all momentum and cohesion. By the time Brunner exploited a dozy mix-up between Milos Kerkez and Federico Chiesa about whose responsibility he was at a corner to flash his header past Mamardashvili, only two of the 22 starters were still on the pitch.

Liverpool: Alisson (Mamardashvili 46), Tsimikas (Kerkez 59), Van Dijk (c) (Chambers 59), Ndukwe (Endo 46), Frimpong (Ramsay 75), Gravenberch (Nyoni 59), Gakpo (Ngumoha 59), Wirtz (McConnell 59), Koumas (Chiesa 75), Isak (Muñoz 59)Substitutes: Morrison, Davies.Goals: Isak (16), Wirtz (29)Monaco: Hradecky, Nazinho (Mawissa 75), Dier (c) (Kehrer 75), S Sané, Vanderson (Teze 46), Golovin (Idumbo 75), Cabral (Soubeir 75), Camara (Benzahra 64), Detourbet (Coulibaly 64), Biereth (Brunner 80), Abline (Konaté 64).Substitutes: Assab, Kohn, Lienard, Nibombe, Touré.  Goals: Golovin (44 pen), Biereth (56), Brunner (88)

They played well in the first half, as they did against Leeds, but lost all shape and structure in the second half to lose 3-2.

Yellow card for Konate for clattering into Endo late. That’s the last of the action.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 3 (Brunner)  Brilliant near-post glancing header from a devilishly whippy, dipping corner. Kerkez doing his best Rip van Winkle impression.

Diligent defensive work by Ngumoha stops Konate’s run down the outside left.

A final substitution, hopefully. Brunner replaces Biereth. Konate’s shot, a pearoller, is easily saved by Mamardashvili after A mix-up between Kerkez and Munoz.

As usual, the substitutions have killed the game. Watched Leeds vs RB Leipzig yesterday. They played two 60 minute matches which kept it more competitive for longer but still descended into a kickabout late on.

Mawissa, Kehrer, Idumbo and Soubeir have replaced Nazinho, Dier, Golovin and Cabral.

Monaco also made changes, four I think. Will catch up with then once they’re confirmed. Ramsey is into the game straight away tp stop Coulibaly’s shot.

Ramsay, Chiesa and Elliott are coming on for Szoboszlai, Frimpong and Koumas. Lovely applause for Elliott.

Konate sweeps a left-foot shot from the left of the box past the right post with Mamardashvili forced into a headlong dive. Liverpool have lost their defensive shape and intensity, allowing Monaco to punch holes through the lines with some direct running.

Nazinho gets round Frimpong down the Monaco left and cuts back the perfect pass to put it on a plate for Coulibaly who hammers a left-foot shot from the right of the D that Mamardashvili throws up his hands to block. That would have stung. Good save. A flag would have meant it wouldn’t have counted but even so Frimpong’s defensive work wasn’t good enough.

It’s been very scrappy since the changes but then Ngumoha pounces on to a loose ball, glides up the right and tries to play Koumas in behind the back four. Sadly, he overhits the pass which trickles out for a goal-kick. Cue an ovation and cries of ‘Rio! Rio!’

Three changes for Monaco with Detoubet, Abline and Camara departing for Benzhara, Coulibaly and Konaté.

Ngumoha has gone to the right wing and Koumas is playing through the middle as a false nine.

Liverpool make five changes with Gakpo, Van Dijk, Wirtz, Tsimikas and Isak departing while Munoz makes his ‘debut’ with Ngumoha, Nyoni, Chambers, McConell and Kerkez.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 2 (Biereth) Mistake by Gravenberch allows Golovin to play a pass into the left half of the box for Biereth. His first shot is well saved by Mamardashvili at full stretch but his tenacity allowed him to get to the rebound ahead of Endo, swivel and stick his second effort in to equalise.

Monaco overplay at the edge of the box, Detourbet, Biereth and Abline playing ‘after you. Claud’, instead of shooting.

A slick, short passing move between Gravenberch, Wirtz and Isak ends with Isak on the deck in the box after Gravenberch’s step-over allowed the ball to run to him. Isak took a touch to move the ball on to his left but gave the defender a glimmer of it and he hacked it away before felling Isak as well as collateral damage.

Quiet start to the half. Biereth just pressed Mamardashvili but the keeper managed to sweep the ball away even though under more pressure than he would have expected.

Liverpool try to play out from the back with Mamardashvili spearing a straight pass to Gravenberch who tried to knock it round the corner for Endo but the ball skidded under his studs and out for a throw-in.

Isak is apparently claiming both goals. Replays are indistinct. He could have clipped it in off his heel as he had a swing at the ball while grounded at the same time as Wirtz.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

Endo has slotted in at centre-back alongside Van Dijk.

Half-time changes: Mamardashvili for Alisson and Endo for Ndukwe.

For Monaco, Teze for Vanderson at right-back.

Much to admire in that first-half performance from Liverpool’s front six and centre-backs, the latter two particularly out of possession and winning it back. The man-to-man system is working well for them. But they should be out of sight by now instead of leading by only a goal.

Liverpool free-kick on the right after a foul on Koumas. Szoboszlai whips in the cross and Van Dijk gets up first to the left of the penalty spot but bludgeons his header about a foot wide of the right post.

Charlie Adam says the penalty was ‘a soft one’ but Van Dijk did not adjust when Golovin shifted it to his right, stuck out a leg and Golovim understandably decided to topple over the hurdle.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 1 (Golovin, pen) Speared it into the top right. Alisson went the right way but was beaten for pace and power.

The referee, Jarred Gillett, gives Monaco a penalty. It was deserved, too. Golovin went on a driving run down the middle, shifted it to his right and was tripped by Van Dijk.

Liverpool are well worth their lead. They are streets ahead of Monaco.

A microcosm of the game so far: Liverpool pass goes astray, a player wins it back – this time Gakpo – by snapping into a tackle before laying it off to his left for the unmarked Tsimikas to skim a low shot about a foot wide of the left post from 25 yards.

Monaco have done very little since that wee salvo in the opening minute but just now Abline was given too much space from distance but whacked his shot into the Kop.

Big cheer from the crowd for Hugo Ekitike

The impressive Koumas diddles Nazinho with a Cruyff turn but then thumps his shot straight into Hradecky’s chest.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 0 (Wirtz) Pass chipped out to Koumas down the right who arcs a cross to the back post. Gakpo meets it with a header back across goal to Isak whose first effort from a couple of yards is blocked but the ball gets stuck under Isak’s falling body and Wirtz is Johnny on the Spot to stab it in from a 18 inches as Dier tried to scramble it away.

Liverpool have been impressive so far but if there has been a weakness it’s still the balance in central midfield defensively. Going forward both Gravenberch and Szobiszlai have dovetailed together well. They win the ball back when Van Dijk steps out and the midfield two fly forward to tee up Koumas for a shot that strikes Dier.

Chance for Wirtz, who opens his body from the left of the D to try to bend a shot into the bottom right corner but fizzes it the wrong side of the post.

It’s been pretty breathless since the goal, Liverpool dozily letting Monaco through the middle before twice cutting Monaco apart in midfield only for Isak to overrun a pass in the box delivered by Wirtz and then Koumas to shoot over.

Liverpool 1 Monaco 0 (Isak) Chip to Gakpo down the left of the box, he clips it first time back to Gravenberch in the D who lays it off to Szoboszlai. Ping-ping-ping. Szoboszlai keeps the tempo high with return, the one in the one-two with Gravenberch who picks out Isak to bury a shot from about 15 yards into the bottom left corner.

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Excellent move from Liverpool, instigated by Ndukwe’s fine tackle on Biereth. He knocks it short to Gravenberch who arrows a 60-yard pass out to Koumas hurtling down the right. He measures his cross perfectly for Gakpo stealing in off the left wing and though he connects powerfully with the meat of his brow, he bashes it straight at the keeper. He was offside in any case, it transpires.

Charlie Adam on co-comms points out that Liverpool are going man-to-man now in classic Iraola/Bielsa style and when the camera goes high you can see it, especially with the full-backs.

Liverpool are carving the middle of the park up with incisive passing. Szoboszlai starts a move that sends Isak down the left of the box. He traps the chip, turns back to face away from goal and taps a pass back to Wirtz who gallops on to it and bends a shot that Hradecky dives low to his left to beat away with a firm left wrist. Frimpong pounces on the rebound and clips a tame effort straight at Hradecky who had quickly restored himself to the vertical.

Van Dijk gobbles up a long pass over Ndukwe, snuffing out any possibility of Biereth getting there first.

Tsimikas is free down the left but overhits his cross on the run when Isak was begging for a cut-back. The left-back went for the back post and ballooned his centre behind, miles beyond Koumas and Wirtz.

Liverpool defend the corner solidly and Frimpong races away on the counter, bombing on to the ball and sprinting into the Monaco half. But his touch is not as sound as his pace and Monaco deal with him when he fluffs his control.

A period of applause in memory of Kevin Keegan ❤️ pic.twitter.com/AkPZG7babe

Liverpool kick off defending the Kop. They roll the ball back to Frimpong who chips a long pass up the right to Koumas who hares on to the pass down the right and crosses, just beyond Isak. Hradecky gathers and bowls the ball out. A mistake by Tisimikas lets Biereth barrel through the inside-right to hammer a shot that Alisson turns behind for a corner.

The crowd applauds in the modern way. My goodness he was a terrific player. Saw him play for Liverpool, Southampton and Newcastle. Absolutely relentless.

Virgil van Dijk has the pennant. Liverpool are wearing all red with the paint splashes of the 1990 kit. Monaco are in a very pale green.

For me it’s a special game, most of the players and people will be ‘it’s [just] a pre-season friendly’, but for me it’s a lot more than this. It will be the first time I have the chance to go out, to feel this stadium and I hope we can also perform well.

It’s a good game for us, because it’s going to be demanding, it’s a team that wants to dominate and they also want to press high so we will see how we are.

I think the cases of Ali[sson], Cody, and Virgil I think it’s their first game. It shouldn’t go longer than 45 minutes, maybe a little bit more if they feel comfortable.

Also for some of the others Ryan, Flo, and Alex, it’s the second game so we have to be aware of those things.

But the league starts in two weeks, so we cannot wait also too much; we have to give them quality minutes.

I think today is going to be a good reference, two games – Monaco and Como – teams that try dominate the game, they are very good in possession, so they will demand us the best without the ball. If we want to control the game and also physical teams, they are probably a very good test.

I hope we are at the level and we can do very good games.

Le 𝐗𝐈 qui débutera cette rencontre face à 𝐋𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥 📋 pic.twitter.com/2cOYRbzUEN

🥳 Feliz aniversário, 𝐅𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐩𝐞 𝐋𝐮𝐢́𝐬! 🎉Notre coach fête aujourd'hui ses 41 ans 🎂 pic.twitter.com/VTd4BQ5rRK

The Reds to take on AS Monaco at Anfield!Watch the match LIVE on All Red Video 📺

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the first of two Liverpool home friendlies after their preseason tour of the United States. Andoni Iraola’s side saw off Wrexham and Sunderland in their first two matches but gave away a two-goal lead at half-time in the final fixture and ended up being beaten 4-2 by Leeds United in Chicago in the last game after multiple changes. What did we learn? Not a huge amount in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, Alisson, Víctor Muñoz, Cody Gakpo and Alexis Mac Allister, the first four of whom are available today other than an ongoing vulnerability from set-pieces and Curtis Jones looking like he is in desperate need of a fresh start.

This afternoon at Anfield they take on AS Monaco who finished seventh in Ligue 1 this season but are under new management with the recruitment of the former Chelsea and Atlético left-back Filipe Luís as head coach. It’s quite the coup for Le Rocher given he led Flamengo to their first Brazilian title in five years, the Copa Libertadores and the Copa do Brasil in his 18 months in charge.

In pre-season so far he has overseen a 5-2 win over fourth-tier AS Saint-Priest, a 2-0 defeat by Sporting Clube, a 2-2 draw with Cercle Bruges and a 1-0 victory over Getafe. They have sold their best player, Maghnes Akliouche, to PSG for £43m and Aladji Bamba to Newcastle for £34m but have so far retained Mamadou Coulibaly and Folarin Balogun, signed and made Ansu Fati’s loan move into a long-term deal.

Iraola may well persevere with Trey Nyoni in midfield who, after his performances on tour, ought to be on the threshold of a breakthrough season and it would be interesting to see him paired with Ryan Gravenberch just behind Dominik Szoboszlai.

Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who played well in America after coming on for the injured Joe Gomez, does not have a UK work permit and will have to go abroad on loan for the season but Jérémy Jacquet, who has yet to feature, was due to have a fitness test this morning and would be a welcome to boost to a squad whose defence still requires significant reinforcements.

#2078. “Scot Will Be There” Parker’s First West Ham Decisions Could Come Within Hours

Claret & Hugh has been informed within the past few moments that incoming West Ham manager Scott Parker is likely to have some input into team selection for tomorrow night’s Championship game against Cardiff City. The former Hammers midfielder is also expected to attend the match, despite Mark Noble being set to take charge on the touchline.

As West Ham confirmed in their official statement earlier today, Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville have been placed in temporary charge of preparations following the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo. However, the information we’ve received suggests that Parker could still have a say in the team that faces Cardiff.

A C&H source told us just moments ago: “Scot will be there and he’ll have some influence on the team even if he can’t do all of it.”

West Ham’s final training session ahead of the match took place earlier today at Rush Green, before Parker had even signed his proposed two-and-a-half-year contract. But that doesn’t mean he will have no input at all, particularly with the new manager expected to be in attendance tomorrow evening.

Being something of a Championship specialist, and of course a former Hammer, Parker will already be familiar with West Ham’s form and performances this season. I suspect he’ll also have a reasonable idea of which players he wants in the team and which ones might benefit from a spell on the sidelines.

As Claret & Hugh revealed earlier today, Parker’s proposed contract is closely tied to West Ham securing promotion this season. With that in mind, there is every reason for him to want to influence proceedings as quickly as possible, even if Noble is the man officially overseeing tomorrow’s game.

And, to be perfectly honest, I don’t think Parker needs to reinvent the wheel to make some immediate improvements.

There are a couple of really easy wins available to the new Irons gaffer, and some of them should be blindingly obvious to anybody who has watched West Ham over the past few months.

Morato was Nuno’s first choice left back.

Firstly, a rousing team talk and a little bit of urgency might be enough to address West Ham’s dreadful starts to games. It was a recurring problem under Nuno Espírito Santo, and one the former manager never seemed capable of fixing. Getting the players motivated and ready to compete from the opening whistle would be a welcome change.

Then there’s the fairly straightforward business of putting round pegs in round holes. For starters, let’s play an actual left-back in the left-back position. That alone would immediately improve the balance of the team rather than continuing to ask players to operate in unfamiliar roles.

Finding the right blend in midfield would also be of huge benefit. West Ham have spent far too much time surrendering control of what is arguably the most important area of the pitch, despite having some talented options available. Getting that balance right could make an enormous difference to the team’s performances.

And finally, there’s Jarrod Bowen. Surely one of the most obvious priorities for any incoming West Ham manager is getting our best attacking player into as many goalscoring positions as possible. Bowen has spent far too much time being asked to produce something out of nothing, and a better-functioning team should make his job considerably easier.

Okay, it’s all a bit paint by numbers, and there’s nothing particularly revolutionary or overly tactical about those suggestions. But that’s rather the point.

West Ham’s problems have often appeared so obvious that you wonder why they’ve been allowed to continue for so long. Parker doesn’t necessarily need weeks on the training ground to recognise them, and even a quick word with the players before kick-off might help address some of the most glaring deficiencies.

Of course, Noble will be responsible for managing the team against Cardiff, and there’s only so much Parker can realistically influence before he’s properly taken charge.

But if the new manager can offer a few sensible suggestions and inject a little urgency into proceedings, I’d suggest that would already be a step in the right direction.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

#2077. Nuno Ignored the Answer to West Ham’s Defensive Crisis

Nuno Espírito Santo has always been described as stubborn by many players and former colleagues, and his continued reluctance to trust either Soungoutou Magassa or Edson Álvarez was becoming increasingly difficult to understand, particularly as West Ham continued to concede soft goals and struggle to protect their back four.

It is a decision, among others, that ultimately contributed to him losing his job.

The issue is not necessarily that West Ham lack talented midfielders. The problem is balance. Too often, the midfield has looked easy to play through, leaving the defence exposed to direct attacks and transition situations. When opposition teams bypass the first line of pressure, the centre-backs are frequently left defending large spaces with insufficient protection in front of them.

That is where Magassa could be invaluable. A converted central defender, the Frenchman is naturally suited to operating as a holding midfielder. His game is built around positioning, breaking up attacks and providing physical presence rather than driving forward or creating chances.

Álvarez offers a slightly different solution. Throughout his career, he has excelled as a midfield shield, winning duels, intercepting passes and protecting defenders. He has also played at centre-back for club and country, underlining his defensive instincts and tactical discipline. While he may lack the mobility to play in a highly expansive system, his ability to sit deep and screen danger is exactly the kind of profile West Ham have often appeared to be missing.

What made Nuno’s stance particularly puzzling is that both players offer something the current squad lacks: specialist defensive security. When a team is leaking goals, managers often look to simplify things, becoming harder to break down before worrying about attacking fluency. Selecting either Magassa or Álvarez in front of the defence could provide that extra layer of protection, reducing the burden on the centre-backs and limiting the number of dangerous situations they face.

Soungoutou Magassa was reinstated to the West Ham squad.

Of course, Nuno saw these players every day in training and may have valid reasons for excluding them. There have been questions over attitude, tactical suitability or future plans, which may all play a part. However, from the outside looking in, West Ham’s defensive record makes it increasingly difficult to justify leaving two natural defensive midfielders on the sidelines while persisting with approaches that continue to leave the back line vulnerable.

Equally, both players are sitting on the wage bill and not playing. In itself, that’s hard to make sense of.

At some point, results have to outweigh previous decisions. If West Ham are serious about tightening up defensively, Magassa and Álvarez look like obvious solutions hiding in plain sight. The question now is whether the interim management will see it?

#2076. Mark Noble Set For New West Ham Role Alongside Scott Parker

Scott Parker’s impending arrival at West Ham United could be accompanied by another interesting appointment, with Mark Noble reportedly set to join his former teammate’s coaching staff. According to The Guardian, Noble is expected to form part of Parker’s backroom team, although the precise role has yet to be officially confirmed.

It’s a development I find particularly encouraging. As Claret & Hugh has already reported, Parker is set to return to the club following the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo, bringing with him an impressive record of three promotions from the Championship.

But the prospect of Parker and Noble working together offers something else entirely. We could have a manager and a senior member of his coaching staff who completely understand West Ham’s identity, what the club means to its supporters and the importance of developing our own players.

For me, this would be a really shrewd move, both politically and in terms of developing West Ham’s younger players. Noble has already been closely involved with the club’s footballing operations as sporting director, giving him valuable knowledge of the youngsters coming through the academy.

There has recently been discussion within West Ham’s recruitment department about improving the pathway between the academy and the first team. Having Noble directly involved in the coaching set-up could be an excellent way of putting that ambition into practice, particularly given his familiarity with the players and their development.

I’d imagine the likes of Lewis Orford, Ollie Scarles and Golambeckis would welcome the prospect of somebody who knows them so well being involved in first-team decisions. That doesn’t guarantee any of them a place, of course, but it should at least help ensure their abilities are properly understood and considered.

There is also something reassuring about the prospect of two former Hammers working together at a time when the club desperately needs a change of direction. Following Nuno’s dismissal, West Ham need to restore confidence and establish a clearer identity on the pitch.

Of course, knowing the club isn’t enough on its own. Parker and Noble will ultimately be judged on results, and the immediate priority remains getting West Ham promoted back to the Premier League.

Nevertheless, I think this would be an excellent appointment. Parker brings his Championship experience, Noble brings his knowledge of West Ham and its young players, and together they could provide exactly the sort of connection between the first team and academy that we’ve been missing.

There’s still the question of Noble’s precise job title and how his sporting director responsibilities would change, but the prospect of the pair working together is one I find genuinely exciting.

#2075. Scott Parker’s Promotion Blueprint Offers West Ham A Way Forward

With Scott Parker set to become West Ham United’s new head coach, I’ve been looking back at his three Championship promotion campaigns to get a better idea of what supporters can expect. Rather than simply guessing how he’ll set up the Hammers, I wanted to examine the formations and players he actually used at Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham.

And having looked through the evidence, I’m increasingly convinced that Parker will favour a 4-2-3-1 at West Ham. It was his preferred system during Burnley’s remarkable 2024/25 promotion campaign, and he also used it at both Bournemouth and Fulham, although he was prepared to switch formations when necessary.

As discussed earlier today, his record of securing promotion with three different clubs was always likely to appeal to West Ham’s decision-makers. But it’s the way he achieved those promotions that interests me, particularly given the problems we’ve witnessed under Nuno Espírito Santo.

Parker’s record is impressive enough without dressing it up. He took Fulham up through the play-offs in 2020, secured automatic promotion with Bournemouth in 2022 and then guided Burnley back to the Premier League with 100 points in 2025.

What I found particularly interesting was that all three sides used a 4-2-3-1 in their final promotion-season matches. That doesn’t mean Parker played the formation every week, but it does provide a useful starting point when trying to establish his tactical preferences.

Those figures show the goals conceded across each 46-match league campaign, rather than just the final matches. And the progression is interesting, with Parker’s most recent promotion-winning team producing by far his strongest defensive record.

However, there’s an important distinction between his Bournemouth and Burnley sides. According to the Premier League’s tactical analysis, Bournemouth actually used 4-3-3 on 27 occasions during their promotion campaign, compared with 13 starts in 4-2-3-1. Parker increasingly favoured the latter towards the end of the season.

Burnley, on the other hand, were much more closely associated with 4-2-3-1. The Premier League’s examination of their promotion campaign identified it as Parker’s first-choice formation, with two midfielders providing defensive protection and the number ten contributing heavily to the press.

To give you lovely C&H readers a clearer picture, I’ve taken the starting elevens from Fulham’s 2020 play-off final victory against Brentford and Burnley’s final Championship fixture against Millwall in 2025.

Both were recorded as 4-2-3-1, although the responsibilities of individual players were not identical.

The obvious similarity is the presence of two central midfielders behind three more advanced players. That’s the aspect of the formation I find particularly appealing for West Ham.

I’ve already seen plenty of people complaining about Parker’s supposedly negative football, but I find that criticism slightly strange when you look at what he achieved at Burnley.

Sixteen goals conceded in 46 Championship games is incredible. Make no mistake about it. His team also recorded 30 clean sheets, a remarkable achievement which helped Burnley finish the season with 100 points.

Burnley scored 69 goals that season, compared with Leeds United’s 95. So there is a legitimate discussion to be had about whether Parker’s football can sometimes be too cautious, but I certainly wouldn’t dismiss the defensive record as a negative.

In fact, I would expect the first priority of any manager arriving at West Ham to be fixing the defence. It’s crap.

There’s a certain irony here, of course. West Ham had the most porous defence in the Premier League when Nuno Espírito Santo arrived last season, and we all remember how Graham Potter’s team seemingly couldn’t defend a corner. Improving that situation was supposed to be one of Nuno’s principal jobs.

Yet in the end, we were left with a pragmatic defensive manager who had seemingly forgotten how to park the bus.

As Nuno’s dismissal following the defeat against West Bromwich Albion demonstrated, the club eventually ran out of patience with performances that were neither defensively convincing nor particularly effective going forward.

I think Parker’s defensive organisation is precisely what West Ham should be looking for now. And if that improved structure can give our more creative players a little extra freedom, then so much the better.

Nuno was brought in to fix Potters awful defence

Looking at Parker’s previous teams, I believe 4-2-3-1 would be a sensible fit for the players he is inheriting at West Ham. The formation provides two central midfielders who can protect the defence, which should immediately help address the problems we’ve had with opponents dominating the middle of the pitch.

But the benefit isn’t purely defensive. Having that protection behind the attacking players should allow them to operate with considerably more freedom, rather than constantly worrying about what happens when possession is lost.

It also provides something I believe West Ham have desperately needed: a proper number ten.

And I don’t mean somebody like Mohamedou Kanté being shoehorned into a false-nine position he’s not equipped for. I mean a genuine playmaker with an eye for a pass, a stepover and a trick, somebody capable of unlocking a defence rather than simply occupying a position on the pitch.

That’s where Divine Mukasa comes into it for me, although I could also see Manor Solomon operating in that role.

I think either could benefit from having two midfielders behind them, particularly if Jarrod Bowen is given the freedom to get into more dangerous attacking positions.

Of course, there’s an important qualification here. Parker’s Burnley number ten was often expected to work extremely hard without the ball, pressing opponents and helping protect the midfield. So it would be wrong to assume he will automatically select a traditional playmaker simply because he uses 4-2-3-1.

Nevertheless, the formation offers that possibility, and I think it’s one West Ham’s attacking players would hopefully enjoy playing in.

There’s another reason I’m reluctant to accept the suggestion that Parker can only produce negative football.

His Bournemouth team were particularly effective at pressing opponents during their promotion season. The Premier League’s tactical analysis recorded them as the Championship’s most intense pressing side by passes per defensive action, with opponents averaging just 10.8 passes before Bournemouth intervened defensively.

That suggests a manager who is capable of setting up a team to win the ball back aggressively, rather than simply sitting deep and hoping to nick a goal.

Bournemouth also conceded only 39 league goals during that campaign, demonstrating that Parker was able to combine a relatively aggressive approach without sacrificing defensive organisation.

And that’s really what I’d like to see at West Ham.

I’m not expecting Parker to turn us into some sort of attacking footballing circus, nor do I think fans should judge him on whether every game produces three or four goals.

But I do expect a team that knows its jobs, defends properly, competes from the first whistle and provides enough attacking support for its better players to make a difference.

The evidence from his previous promotion campaigns suggests Parker is capable of delivering that sort of structure. Whether he can reproduce it at West Ham remains to be seen, but there are genuine reasons for optimism.

Three promotions with three different clubs, a remarkable defensive record at Burnley and a clear history of using systems that could suit West Ham’s attacking players.

For me, that’s a far more useful way of assessing Scott Parker than simply dismissing him as a negative manager before he’s even started.

#2074. ‘On another day…’ – Ex-PGMOL chief says Liverpool were ‘fortunate’ with one decision on Sunday

A former Premier League referee believes that Liverpool were ‘fortunate’ with one incident in particular from their defeat to Arsenal on Sunday.

The Reds were left incensed by the failure of referee Andy Madley and VAR Stuart Attwell to spot a clear shirt tug by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak inside the penalty area, a decision that Steven Gerrard lamented as ‘an absolute embarrassment‘.

It has even prompted debate as to whether the Swedish striker – who stayed on his feet and didn’t protest – could’ve done more to influence the officials, but earlier in the match there was an incident which had the Gunners complaining.

Inside the opening minute, Trey Nyoni caught Martin Odegaard on the Achilles but avoided a yellow card, just as he did for a foul on Kai Havertz shortly afterwards.

Former PGMOL chief executive Keith Hackett feels that the Liverpool midfielder was quite lucky not to have been at least booked over those two early fouls, especially the first one.

He told Football Insider: “First of all, it doesn’t matter whether it’s the first or the 90th minute; the laws of the game apply. For me, if you like, the least amount of punishment on that is a yellow card. I think that challenge is reckless.

“On another day… and because it is early, I think that’s why he’s fortunate not to get a red. He’s raked his studs down the Achilles of his opponent.

“However you look at that, that has to receive a sanction; so for me, I’ll give him slight benefit of the doubt, slight mistiming, whatever you want, but he has to come out of that with a yellow card at the very minimum.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Taking the challenge on Odegaard in isolation, Nyoni probably should’ve been booked for the nature of the foul, irrespective of it being in the first minute. We acknowledge that the Liverpool youngster got away with one there.

Would he have flown into the tackle on Havertz had he already been on a yellow card? Maybe not, but to us it’s one of those where a word of warning from Madley would’ve sufficed.

In that scenario, we suspect that Andoni Iraola may have substituted the 19-year-old much earlier than the 59th minute, for fear that the midfielder was a red card in waiting and was showing a bit too much enthusiasm on his first Premier League start.

Nyoni and Liverpool were lucky in that instance, but don’t let this be a case of two wrongs making a right when weighing it up against the penalty we should’ve had for Timber’s shirt tug on Isak.

Football stakeholders are right to demand higher standards of officiating at top-flight level, and the onus is on Pro Ref chief executive Howard Webb to ensure that his referees do better.

#2073. West Ham’s big guns come out with verdict over Scott Parker appointment

Whilst officially West Ham United head into the midweek fixture against Cardiff City without a head coach, the Irons will mix the talents of established coaching duo Gerard Prenderville and Steve Potts with the expertise of sporting director Mark Noble to provide the off-field leadership for tonight’s attempt to arrest their two-game losing run and put some points on the board.

It will be intriguing to see the immediate impact which the sacking of Nuno Epirito Santo has on the Hammers’ dressing room when the whistle blows tonight.

Hopefully that means the end of ‘outcast’ squad members and that players will get utilised within their established positions soon enough, so that the era of square pegs being pushed into round holes is finally ended.

Many will feel relieved that the days of the division of the Hammers’ squad are ended: Now perhaps the handbrake could come off for the careers of several ‘outcasts’.

Behind the scenes the appointment of Scott Parker does seem nailed on, whilst no official pronouncement has yet been made. All roads point to the former Hammer of the Year taking control of the West Ham squad, which is an appointment that has already been welcomed by former players – one a former assistant to David Moyes who is, of course, still pretty close to the club.

Kevin Nolan, former captain during West Ham’s last promotion winning campaign, pronounced judgement on TalkSPORT:

“I’m delighted with the talk that it’s Scotty going in, giving a young British manager an opportunity at a big club. He’s got a track record. It’s going to be a tough season”

Former Irons’ striker turned TV pundit Dean Ashton was similarly positive. Speaking on talksport, Ashton pointed out that West Ham supporters hadn’t had a manager who felt connected with them for many years, but all that would change if and when Parker is confirmed:

“They want to be inspired again. It is important to connect again with the supporters… He’s certainly got fire in his belly and will relish the opportunity to manage West Ham.”

Whilst some fans profess disappointment over the ‘low ambition’ shown by the football club in considering Scott Parker, I’d suggest they’ve picked exactly the right man to do the job.

Forget the long term. Climb the greasy pole out of this hugely challenging division at all costs and back in the Premier League first. Then worry about what kind of football you want to play.

Because failure carries unthinkable financial repercussions for this football club. Right now, I’d suspect on track records alone, there’s nobody better qualified than former West Ham captain Scott Parker to do the job required.

#2072. Ex-Celtic star backs 'amazing' former boss to deliver amid growing pressure

Vidar Riseth believes Celtic should stick with Martin O’Neill and has backed his former boss to mastermind a huge European result against Besiktas.

The Norwegian played under O’Neill during his first spell at Parkhead and remains convinced the 74-year-old is the right man to steer the Hoops through their current difficulties.

Speaking to SunSport, Riseth insists Celtic are fortunate to have a manager of O’Neill’s calibre in the dugout as he urged the club hierarchy to keep faith with him.

O’Neill is under increasing pressure following six defeats in Celtic’s last ten matches and desperately needs a victory against Besiktas to keep their slim hopes of reaching the Europa League knockout stage alive.

“It doesn’t surprise me he is still going at his age. As long as Martin can talk and can sit in the dugout, he will do a good job because he’s an amazing guy.

Their difficulties have continued in the Europa League, where three defeats have left Celtic 35th in the 36-team league phase. However, Riseth insists there is still time for O’Neill and his players to salvage their campaign.
